st.headline: Democrats’ midterm sweep puts AI boom to the test – with much at stake for Asia
st.teaser: With tech stocks rallying after the vote, markets appear to be betting on a more measured build-out.
fullText: SINGAPORE – The Democratic Party’s unexpected takeover of both chambers of the US Congress is giving way to renewed debate on what the future holds for the AI infrastructure build-out.

For Singapore and other Asian economies riding the AI investment boom, the key question after the Democrats’ US midterm sweep is whether tighter scrutiny will derail data centre spending or impose the financial discipline investors want.
With technology stocks rallying after the vote, markets appear to be betting on a more measured build-out rather than an abrupt slowdown.

Beyond US interest rates , bond yield s and tariff s , the election’s biggest implication for Asian exports, including Singapore’s, is its potential impact on the AI boom, which has become a major growth drive r.

If Democrats, who are mostly sceptical about artificial intelligence, take an aggressive policy approach towards the construction of new data centres, the much-feared scenario of a sharp pull-back in economic growth and a financial market upheaval may yet be possible.
However, there is optimism that things may not go that far.

In fact, the unexpected scale of the Democratic victory is giving way to an even more surprising rally in tech stocks, the opposite of what was expected over the past month, when stocks of Big Tech hyperscalers were hammered.

The US tech benchmark Nasdaq Composite rose 1.44% on Nov 4, the day after the midterms, after having suffered a massive sell-off over the past month. Shares of Google’s parent Alphabet surged 3.25%, Microsoft rose 6.68% and Amazon was up 6.1%.

Regardless, the market expects Democratic gains in key state capitols – including governorships, Senate and House seats in some of President Donald Trump’s Republican Party’s strongholds – to trigger restrictions on data centres, such as conditional moratoria over water, noise and high electricity demands.

But a higher hurdle to AI build-out may not be entirely bad. In fact, new restrictions may moderate the pace of the build-out and ease investor and shareholder concerns around the enormous capital expenditures by hyperscalers.
The market appears to be betting that while Congress could increase oversight and restrict new incentives for AI data centres, sweeping regulatory legislation would still face a presidential veto.
And if tech firms respond by showing fiscal discipline, investors would get the chance to pick outstanding performers.
Charu Chanana, Singapore-based chief investment strategist at Danish investment bank Saxo, said the US election has accelerated a reassessment of AI that was already under way.

“The sector entered the midterms with elevated valuations, enormous capital expenditure commitments and growing investor concerns about how quickly AI investments will translate into profits,” she said.

Increased regulatory scrutiny by a Democratic Congress could further accelerate investors’ shift from broad AI exposure towards companies with strong cash flows, pricing power and visible returns on investment, she noted.

“Investors should distinguish between three things: the immediate reaction to a political surprise, the policies that could realistically change, and the underlying corporate fundamentals,” Chanana added.

Bernard Yaros, deputy chief US economist at Britain -based research firm Oxford Economics, said risks to the AI build-out lie more with state and local policy, as state governors, utility regulators and zoning boards control rates, incentives, permitting and grid access.
Hence, a worst-case scenario would be a simultaneous tightening of data centre policies in the US South and Midwest, which are the country’s biggest regional drivers for future construction.
“That said, there are strong incentives to avoid policies that would severely disrupt data centre construction,” he added.

Yaros said data centres are increasingly framed as a national security priority and the AI investment cycle has become a meaningful source of economic growth, as these projects bring tax revenue and construction jobs that state and local officials would be reluctant to forgo.
Near-term investment is likely to remain resilient, but restrictions on new projects could become a more meaningful headwind to the AI investment boom from 2028.

Robert St Clair, managing director and head of investment strategy at Temasek-linked Fullerton Fund Management, said that over time, the Democrats may push for less favourable policy supports for certain AI-linked infrastructure and data centres, as well as seek stronger guardrails to avoid any adverse impacts from the technology on society and jobs.

However, US AI-related infrastructure investment is already growing rapidly, with a robust pipeline of projects planned for the years ahead. Hence, it is unclear how significant a headwind any potential policy changes could prove, he said.
If Big Tech dials back its capital borrowing , there will likely be some easing in bond yields as well.
But the major impact on bond yields and possibly Federal Reserve interest rates may come from a divided government that hamstrings federal spending.
Chanana said that while existing tax legislation will not disappear, new tax cuts or major spending packages would become harder for the Trump administration to pass.

Government funding will lapse after Dec 11, before the new Congress starts on Jan 3. A rapid reconciliation Bill focused on defence during the lame-duck session is a near-term risk for the bond market to watch.
On tariffs, Trump will retain substantial executive authority.
Hence, Yaros said, the risk is that his administration will become more aggressive on trade issues.

He added that the US-China trade truce will also be top of mind in the new year. The latest truce is set to expire on Jan 10, which will bring both countries back to the negotiating table. If they fail to extend the truce, Trump may seek to use the pending Section 301 investigation into overcapacity to impose a fresh round of tariffs on China.

cna.headline: Sony posts 45% Q2 profit rise on movies, games boost
cna.teaser: Sony posts 45% Q2 profit rise on movies, games boost
fullText: TOKYO, Nov 5 : Sony on Thursday reported a 45 per cent rise in second-quarter operating profit of 622.3 billion yen ($3.95 billion), beating market estimates, due to stronger performance at its games and movies units.

Contributors to the stronger performance, which led the Japanese entertainment and technology conglomerate to hike its full-year profit outlook by 9 per cent, included the hit movie "Spider-Man: Brand New Day".
Sony's games business is expected to be a major beneficiary of the launch of "Grand Theft Auto VI" on November 19 but is grappling with higher memory chip prices due to the AI boom.
Companies continue to be squeezed by elevated memory prices, with iPhone maker Apple this week flagging pressure on margins over the holiday quarter.
Our chief editor shares analysis and picks of the week's biggest news every Saturday.

listening.title: Singapore Expands Green Corridor Initiative
listening.transcript: Singapore has announced an ambitious urban design plan aimed at extending pedestrian pathways across several central districts. City planners hope the expanded green corridors will reduce heat while encouraging active mobility among residents. Community feedback has been overwhelmingly positive, with citizens welcoming shaded connection routes between parks. Construction on the first phase is scheduled to commence early next year.

economistArticle.title: What markets make of the midterms
paras: When American voters handed Democrats a series of unexpected victories in the midterm elections, political commentators scrambled to rewrite their narratives. Yet across trading desks in New York and London, reaction was muted. Stock indexes barely budged, while bond yields shifted only imperceptibly. Investors, it seems, greeted the surprising political outcome with a collective yawn.

Part of this nonchalance stems from gridlock, which equity markets historically favor. Even with Democrats holding key positions, a divided Congress curtails ambitious legislative initiatives. Wall Street generally prefers policy stagnation to sweeping statutory overhauls that introduce regulatory uncertainty. For major corporations, gridlock implies fewer fiscal surprises and a lower likelihood of sudden corporate tax hikes.

Furthermore, investor attention remains firmly anchored on macroeconomics rather than partisan politics. The Federal Reserve's monetary stance, persistent inflation, and global supply constraints exert far greater influence on equity valuations than congressional committee chairs. Traders recognize that central bank policies will dictate capital allocation long after electoral banners are packed away.

Currency markets similarly mirrored this tranquility. The dollar index traded within a narrow band, reflecting the view that macroeconomic fundamentals remain the true drivers of foreign exchange sentiment. Sovereign bond yields, too, remained stable, indicating that debt markets perceive little immediate threat to fiscal stability.

Ultimately, the market response underscores a practical reality: political drama makes compelling television, but earnings reports and interest rates drive asset prices. Until fiscal policy threatens to destabilize macroeconomic balance, financial markets will continue to treat midterm results as secondary noise.
economistArticle.cn:
当美国选民在中期选举中赋予民主党一系列出人意料的胜利时，政治评论员们纷纷忙着重写分析逻辑。然而，在纽约和伦敦的交易室里，市场的反应却十分平静。股票指数几乎没有波动，而债券收益率也微乎其微地移动。投资者们似乎以集体打哈欠的方式迎来了这一意外结果。
这种冷淡的一部分原因在于政治僵局，而股票市场历史性地偏爱僵局。即便民主党保住了关键席位，一个分化分裂的国会也会限制有雄心的立法计划。华尔街通常更倾向于政策停滞，而不是带来监管不确定性的激进法律改革。对于大型企业而言，政治僵局意味着更少的财政意外，以及突然上调企业税的可能性降低。
此外，投资者的注意力依然紧紧锚定在宏观经济而非党派政治上。美联储的货币政策立场、持续的通胀以及全球供应限制对股票估值的影响，远大于国会各委员会主席的人选。交易员们意识到，在选举横幅被收起很久之后，央行政策仍将决定资本的配置方向。
汇率市场同样反映了这种平静。美元指数在狭窄区间内交易，这表明宏观经济基本面仍是外汇市场情绪的真正主导力量。主权债券收益率也保持稳定，表明债务市场认为财政稳定性不会受到直接威胁。
归根结底，市场的反应强调了一个务实的现实：政治戏剧适合制作引人入胜的电视节目，但盈利报告和利率才是驱动资产价格的根本因素。在财政政策威胁到打破宏观经济平衡之前，金融市场将继续把中期选举结果视为次要噪音。
